title: Uptown saloons, the Pigpen and street-corner blues
summary: No music in neighborhood saloons; the Pigpen where professionals played for a dollar and a half; Louis Armstrong did not play Bourbon Street; blues from pianos and records.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Cabarets, honky-tonks and the Storyville nightlife scene

blocks.x: mother's side. Yeah. Mm-hmm. Anyway, I have a lot more to ask you. Were there any saloons in your neighborhood? You said you played at different places, but would you play at places in your neighborhood?

No, no. There were saloons in the neighborhood, but they didn't have any music. Now, there was music downtown, and some of the places uptown, like the Pigpen. Did you go to the Pigpen? Oh, I went there once. Now those are the players who played, like the Pigpen and some of those old places, Louis Armstrong played there. See, a lot of people think that Louis Armstrong played on Bourbon Street. Because people come in and ask me, they say, oh, did Louis Armstrong play here? No. And when he played at Preservation Heart, I said, no, he didn't play on Bourbon Street at all. There wasn't no Bourbon. Bourbon Street didn't have entertainment at that time. Yeah. But they think that Louis Armstrong played in the French Quarter. And when Louis Armstrong learned how to play well enough to make some money, he left and went to Chicago. King Oliver was sitting for him to come to Chicago, Joe Oliver. And he stayed in Chicago until he moved to New York. When he left Chicago, he left King Oliver Band and went to New York to play
with Fletcher Henderson. Well, you mentioned the Pigpen. Did you ever, that was on Decatur Street?
No, the Pigpen was on Liberty and Phillip. Liberty and Phillip. Okay.
Uptown, Uptown Street. All right. This, what year is this?

Now, this, in around 1933, 32, 33, is when I went there. But, uh. What kind of place was it? Just a dance hall? It wasn't anything polished. It was just like a dive. But that was the only place that we had to go to have entertainment. I mean, if you didn't go to one of those places, you'd go to a house where they used to have those fish fries. Like, did you ever hear that number, Saturday night, fish fries? Sure. Sure, Louie Jugg. Well, who was playing at the
Pigpen? Did you play at the Pigpen? I played there once, with Professor Victor's band. But

that's where the old, I mean, that's where the professional musicians played. Now what I mean by professional musicians, the guys who were playing for the big money, a dollar and a half a night. Right. Were these dances they played for? Yeah, dances, yeah. Dances. Sometimes I think about the money that they paid us, and the money that the musicians were, and they were glad to make that money. Some of them used to play for nothing. There are some places where the guys used to go and play for drinks. Sure. They played for drinks. Did you hear a lot of piano players? Oh yeah.
